sources.title: Desiderius Erasmus (Q43499), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-06): English label 'Erasmus', description 'Dutch Renaissance humanist, Catholic priest, and theologian (1466-1536)', Korean label 데시데리위스 에라스뮈스, born 28 October 1466 (other values 6 November 1466 and 1469 also listed), died 12 July 1536, country of citizenship the Seventeen Provinces. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Desiderius Erasmus' (first published 2017, substantive revision 2025; introduction, the life and works section and the methodology section read). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: Christian humanism and learned piety; the call 'ad fontes'; a pioneering Greek New Testament that shows text-critical principles; success in literature, education, religion and theology; bestsellers Praise of Folly, Adages, Handbook of the Christian Soldier; the 1516 edition was hastily assembled on his publisher Froben's urging from the manuscripts he could consult, praised by humanists and attacked by theologians; four revised editions (1519, 1522, 1527, 1531) with expanded notes; editions of Jerome, Augustine, Chrysostom and Origen, in many cases the first reliable critical text; for some years he refused to endorse any religious party and published the free-will Diatribe against Luther reluctantly in 1524; moved to Leuven then Basel, and in 1529 to Freiburg; works placed on the Index. Modern scholarly overview, balanced, with the critics' side stated.

Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Erasmus' (the freely visible first half read: life up to his Basel work on the 1516 New Testament and the revision that followed; the rest is behind a subscription wall and was not read). Calls him the greatest scholar of the northern Renaissance and the first editor of the New Testament; his independent stance made him a target of suspicion for partisans on both sides; he expanded the Adages into a work of over 3,000 entries for Aldus's press that first made him famous; Praise of Folly written in More's house; the conviction that 'ancient theology' required mastery of Greek; his own mistakes as a textual critic alongside a 'towering' place in the history of scholarship; conservative theologians at Leuven resisted. Reference article, admiring but notes his errors.

Encyclopaedia Britannica, eleventh edition (1911), 'Erasmus, Desiderius' by Mark Pattison and Percy Stafford Allen (Wikisource transcription, read in part: the Italy and Venice period, the Basel years, the polemics and the assessment). An older, critical historiography: he did the work of two men at Venice writing and correcting proof together; by pensions and gifts he could refuse offers that would have compromised his independence; his sarcasm and quarrels (including with Budé) drew exasperation, a contemporary calling him extremely thin-skinned; argues that his neutrality came from the reasonableness of his nature rather than timidity, while noting that opponents called him a trimmer; judges the Greek Testament to have no critical value as an edition yet profound influence because it was first and exposed Vulgate errors. Contradicts the modern view on the text's scholarly value.

Museum of the Bible collection record 'Novum Instrumentum Omne, Erasmus's New Testament' (Basel: Froben, 1516; page read in full). Says he was the first to prepare a complete Greek New Testament for publication, presenting his own Latin translation and critical notes; the hurried work was done in just ten months and resulted in hundreds of typesetting errors; from the second edition onward it was titled Novum Testamentum. Museum catalogue entry, with a provenance history of the museum's copy.

William Andrews Clark Memorial Library (UCLA), Tudor collection title-list entry 'Novum Instrumentum omne' (page read in full). In England he took Lord Mountjoy as pupil, met More and Colet, set about learning Greek and began a new Greek-to-Latin translation of the Gospels and Epistles; Colet lent manuscripts from St Paul's; he used four partial Greek manuscripts in Cambridge and five in Basel; the Complutensian Greek text was printed first (1514) but delayed until 1522 by papal privilege; his Greek text is clearly inferior to the Alcala text, but his reputation, priority in the market and low cost led to wide distribution and long-lasting influence on biblical scholarship. Library description, balanced on quality.

Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam, linked-art record for object RP-P-OB-1281, 'Portret van Erasmus' (Imago Erasmi Roterodami ab Alberto Durero ad vivam effigiem deliniata), engraving by Albrecht Dürer dated MDXXVI with monogram AD, 249 x 193 mm (record opened live; the museum states the date, title and monogram are engraved on the object and carries a Public Domain Mark and a CC0 right). Used for the portrait only, not as support for any row.

independent_thinking.rationale: [src_erasmus_sep, src_erasmus_britannica, src_erasmus_eb1911 | 1516-1536 | modern scholarly overview, reference article, older critical historiography] The SEP says that for some years he refused to endorse any religious party, reluctantly published his 1524 Discussion of Free Will against Luther, and took a sceptical stance on the clarity of Scripture; Britannica says his rejection of both predestination and papal claims made partisans on both sides suspicious; Pattison and Allen argue it was reasonableness, not timidity, though opponents called him a trimmer. The pattern is consistent but is a historians' characterisation of a stance, and it cost him support on both sides, so the impact is mixed.

execution_speed.rationale: [src_erasmus_mob, src_erasmus_sep, src_erasmus_eb1911 | 1508-1516 | museum catalogue, modern scholarly overview, older historiography] The Museum of the Bible says the 1516 New Testament was done in just ten months with hundreds of typesetting errors; the SEP says he hastily assembled the text on his publisher's urging; Pattison and Allen say he did the work of two men at Venice, writing and correcting proof at once. Speed is documented, but the same sources tie it to errors, so the impact is mixed and confidence is kept below 0.5.

mastery_orientation.rationale: [src_erasmus_clark, src_erasmus_sep, src_erasmus_britannica | 1499-1531 | library description, modern scholarly overview, reference article] The Clark Library says that after meeting More and Colet he undertook to learn Greek to move study of Scripture beyond scholastic disputes, and drew on nine manuscripts in Cambridge and Basel; the SEP lists four revised editions of the New Testament (1519 to 1531) with corrections and expanded notes and editions of Jerome, Augustine, Chrysostom and Origen; Britannica adds his conviction that mastery of Greek was needed. The sustained deepening of one craft is documented; the motive is read from the pattern.

cross_domain_range.rationale: [src_erasmus_sep, src_erasmus_britannica | 1500-1531 | modern scholarly overview, reference article] The SEP says he succeeded in four genres (literature, education, religion, theology) and reports his own 1523 catalogue grouping his writings under nine headings, from language handbooks and the Adages to patristic editions and polemics; Britannica adds classical literature, satire, educational theory and works on princes and peace. The breadth is documented; the 1523 catalogue is his own list as reported by the SEP. RUBRIC_CORRECTION (lead review, before eligibility): cross_domain_range lowered from 72 / 0.54 to 68 / 0.48 because the SEP and his own 1523 catalogue (self-report) carry the breadth.

collaboration.rationale: [src_erasmus_sep, src_erasmus_clark, src_erasmus_eb1911 | 1499-1521 | modern scholarly overview, library description, older historiography] The SEP says he collaborated with More on translations of Lucian and widened his New Testament project at Froben's urging; the Clark Library says Colet lent him manuscripts from St Paul's; Pattison and Allen say he handled business of Froben's press, sending couriers. Documented cooperation with a few named people; the same sources describe sharp quarrels with rivals, so the row stays modest.

autonomy_need.rationale: [src_erasmus_eb1911, src_erasmus_britannica, src_erasmus_sep | 1517-1536 | older historiography, reference article, modern scholarly overview] Pattison and Allen say that, supported by pensions and gifts, he could refuse proposals that would have interfered with his cherished independence; Britannica calls his stance independent; the SEP says he held out for years against endorsing any party. The explicit claim about refusing proposals comes from one 1911 source, and his reliance on patrons cuts both ways. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): top-risk row; confidence lowered from 0.48 to 0.42 (score unchanged) because the central statement rests on one older source and patronage complicates the reading.

portrait.source: Engraving 'Imago Erasmi Roterodami ab Alberto Durero ad vivam effigiem deliniata' by Albrecht Dürer, dated MDXXVI (1526) and monogrammed AD, in the Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam (object number RP-P-OB-1281). The plate's own lettering names the sitter and says the image was drawn from life; the file is the museum's full-image scan (original 2894 x 3736 pixels) downscaled to 929 x 1200 with no upscaling.
portrait.license: Public Domain Mark 1.0 on the museum's image and a CC0 right on the museum's record, as read live; the work is a 1526 engraving by an artist who died in 1528.
portrait.attribution: Albrecht Dürer, Portrait of Erasmus of Rotterdam, engraving, 1526. Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam, RP-P-OB-1281 (Public Domain). Downscaled.
portrait.creator: Albrecht Dürer (engraver and designer)

provenance.notes: portrait_preflight: STRONG (lead-robust) (lead) / CONFIRMED with a different Rijksmuseum print chosen: the lead opened RP-P-1907-2611 (a 19th-century wood engraving by Jean Guillaume after a drawing by Eustache L'Orsay after Holbein, dated by the museum 1832-1893, PDM + CC0) and I re-opened it, but preferred a lifetime engraving, Dürer's RP-P-OB-1281 of 1526, as the better-documented image (the sitter named on the plate, a famous artist, no copy-of-copy chain). PORTRAIT RIGHTS: Rijksmuseum linked-art record id.rijksmuseum.nl/200122345 opened live: PDM on the image service and CC0 on the record; museum records the engraved date 'MDXXVI', monogram 'AD' and title 'IMAGO ERASMI....' as mentioned on the object; no conflicting museum notice (holder_contradiction_found false). IMAGE INSCRIPTION CHECK (looked at the 1549 x 2000 scan): the cartouche reads 'IMAGO ERASMI ROTERODAMI AB ALBERTO DVRERO AD VIVAM EFFIGIEM DELINIATA', then Greek 'THN KPEITTΩ TA ΣΥΓΓΡΑΜΜΑΤΑ ΔΕΙΞΕΙ', then 'MDXXVI' and the AD monogram; the figure is a bonneted scholar writing at a lectern with books; the lettering names Erasmus of Rotterdam and Dürer, no contradiction (lesson from the Roster65 Muteferrika print applied). KIND: historical_depiction, deliberately conservative: the inscription claims the likeness was drawn from life and Dürer is known to have drawn him, but I did not verify an independent record of a sitting, and the engraving is a later rendition (1526). PREFLIGHT: QID VERIFIED LIVE (2026-11-06, Wikidata API) Q43499 label 'Erasmus', description 'Dutch Renaissance humanist, Catholic priest, and theologian (1466-1536)', ko label 데시데리위스 에라스뮈스 (also the Korean Wikipedia title); not in prod66.json (slug, name, aliases and QID checked); no candidate file existed. REGION western_europe (Dutch; Boulton, Hume and Schopenhauer precedents; he worked in Leuven, Basel, Freiburg and England). ERA early_modern. BIRTH YEAR 1466 follows Wikidata's first value and the lead; the SEP gives 28 October 1469 citing recent scholarship, Britannica 1469 [1466?], the 1911 article 1466, the Museum of the Bible 1466: sources disagree and rows do not depend on it. ZERO POLITICS: primary identity scholar, writer and theologian; his church-politics roles (the Luther polemic, the Leuven and Paris censures, his honorary councillor post to Charles V, peace tracts) are context only; the Diatribe is scored as an intellectual stance on one row with the caveat, and no political leadership, advisory or diplomatic role is scored. VOCABULARY: occupations scholar, theologian and writer; fields literature, education and religion; tags renaissance and prolific; archetype scholarly_specialist; impact domains literary, educational, cultural and historical; all labelled in en.ts and ko.ts (grepped). KO NAME: the Wikidata and Korean Wikipedia label is the long 데시데리위스 에라스뮈스; the standard short form 에라스뮈스 is used as display name per the 'short' rule. CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry on Erasmus (https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/erasmus/). READ (6 sources besides Wikidata, 5 for behaviour): SEP (introduction, life and works, methodology); Britannica (free first half); 1911 Britannica by Pattison and Allen (in part); Museum of the Bible record; Clark Library entry; Rijksmuseum record (portrait only). PERSPECTIVES: (1) modern scholarly overview (SEP); (2) older critical historiography (Pattison and Allen 1911) which COUNTERS the modern view on the Greek text's value and on his character (thin-skinned, sarcastic, quarrelsome) and defends him against the charge of timidity; (3) institutional catalogue entries on the 1516 edition (Museum of the Bible, Clark Library) that stress haste, errors and inferiority to the Alcala text; (4) reference article (Britannica). NON-SELF BEHAVIOURAL SOURCES: all of them; SELF MATERIAL: none used directly (the 1523 catalogue of his writings appears only as reported by the SEP and is labelled as his own list in the row). NOT OPENED: Erasmus's own letters and works (Collected Works of Erasmus; self-report), Huizinga's 1924 biography, Allen's Opus epistolarum, Rummel and Schoeck monographs, the Renaissance and Reformation article on his leaving Basel (bot-walled), the second half of the Britannica article (paywall), the PC(USA) history page (404), the Catholic Encyclopedia (404). CONTRADICTIONS: priority of the Greek New Testament (SEP: first to reach the market; Museum of the Bible: first complete edition prepared for publication; Clark Library: the Complutensian text was printed first in 1514 but released in 1522); value of the edition (SEP: pioneering text-critical principles; Britannica: mistakes but a towering figure; 1911: no critical value as an edition); the scale of the Adages (over 3,000 entries in Britannica and the 1911 article, over 4,000 in the SEP's later enlarged form); so no row claims a first. HONEST LIMITS: pre-modern evidence is sparse and mostly interpretive; six rows only, confidence at most 0.54; the SEP and Britannica are friendly, the 1911 article and the library entries supply the critical counter-voice. EXCLUSIONS: no politics, no church-political roles, no private life, no personality inference from his illegitimate birth or monastic vows; no legend. MAJOR ACHIEVEMENT GATE: first pass PASS on primary, top-omission, identity, significance-over-novelty and side-project checks (the 1516 Greek New Testament and the northern humanist scholarship, the Adages and Praise of Folly, and the patristic editions with the philosophy of Christ are the cards).
